title: Could microlending develop the world?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the American century, US dominance in the twentieth century, and whether American influence is declining, touching on the American dream and Thomas Friedman's Golden Arches theory. The main segment explains microlending: small loans to entrepreneurs excluded from traditional banks, Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank, social-pressure repayment with weekly collections by bankers on bicycles, a roughly 97 percent repayment rate, nonprofit (Kiva) and for-profit (MicroPlace) lending models, and criticism including unclear impact on poverty and predatory lenders like Banco Azteca in Mexico that lobbied to avoid disclosure of loan terms. The episode closes with listener mail from Stephen Bram of Alliteration, a small business in Newark, Delaware, that sent signs for the studio, and sign-off requests for mail.

segments.title: Opening banter on the American century
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss US dominance in the twentieth century, GDP growth, current wars and the declining dollar, and whether the American century is over, with the American dream and the Golden Arches theory raised.

segments.title: What microlending is and why startup capital is hard to get
segments.summary: Microlending is defined by the borrower's profile rather than loan size. Traditional banks exclude the working poor who lack collateral, credit history or education, so microlenders fill that gap.

segments.title: Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank
segments.summary: Muhammad Yunus, a Bangladeshi economist, founded Grameen Bank in the nineties to lend to the poor, women and the illiterate without collateral, sending agents to rural villages. He won the Nobel Peace Prize.

segments.title: Social pressure and weekly repayment
segments.summary: Grameen relies on social pressure and family reputation to ensure repayment, with weekly payments collected by bankers on bicycles who are often neighbors. Microlending repayment is cited at about 97 percent.

segments.title: Kiva and MicroPlace: nonprofit and for-profit lending
segments.summary: Kiva is a nonprofit model where people contribute as little as twenty-five dollars to borrowers' business plans, with gift certificates available and no interest returned. MicroPlace is a for-profit model offering yields up to about five percent. Mutual funds also invest in microlenders.

segments.title: Criticism: loan sharks and predatory lenders
segments.summary: Microlenders compete with loan sharks, though microloan interest is much lower. Banco Azteca in Mexico, founded by a retail magnate, charges high rates and lobbied to be exempt from disclosing loan terms. Other large banks are also named as investors in such lenders.

segments.title: Whether microlending reduces poverty and conflict
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether microloans actually fund intended businesses, and whether poverty drives terrorism, globalization prevents war, and the evidence is still unclear.

segments.title: Listener mail from Stephen Bram of Alliteration
segments.summary: Stephen Bram of Alliteration in Newark, Delaware, sent the hosts signs for their studio. The hosts thank him and share his business contact information.

segments.title: Sign-off and how to contact the show
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to send mail and point to HowStuffWorks.com for related articles on economics.
